original_paragraph: Days on market is the clearest published test of whether a yacht is priced to sell: a buyer should read any listing’s time on market and price-reduction history against the most recent published median for its size band, and note the date of that median. The latest figures for yachts of 24m and above are Northrop & Johnson’s, for the third quarter of 2026. Yachts sold in that quarter had been listed for an average of 445 days, against 542 in the second quarter. Asking prices were cut 1,949 times between January and September, up 7.2 percent on the same months of 2025, and yachts cut in the third quarter had been on the market for a median of 386 days. Neither figure is a size-band median, and a cut asking price is not the final discount. Shorter selling times alongside more frequent price cuts suggest a market dividing on price: yachts priced close to what buyers will pay sell, and the rest wait and are cut.

original_paragraph: The yard-side pattern, less covered in trade press, has recurred through the 2020s: a yard runs into financial difficulty mid-build, and the owner is presented with a choice that is not really a choice. original_paragraph: The buyer pays stage payments forward; when the yard’s financial condition deteriorates, those stage payments become creditor positions in someone else’s insolvency. Refund guarantees protect a portion of the exposure in principle; in practice, particularly under non-tier-one bank wrappers, they are less reliable than the contract suggests. Norton Rose Fulbright’s commentary on Chinese-bank refund guarantees expiring within one month of cancellation is widely cited; the timing of insolvency proceedings rarely lines up with the guarantee window. Benjamin Maltby, a partner at Keystone Law, sets out what separates a reliable guarantee: a bank of high credit standing, preferably independent of the yard and its group; payment on written demand without investigating the dispute; all instalments covered, with interest; validity running to delivery plus a margin. Even then it repays only the sums paid, not lost use, financing costs, or owner-supplied items, and it responds only to a valid termination and a correctly presented demand. The instrument is also rarer and more fragile than buyers assume. “The majority of shipyards simply don’t have the credit lines available to them to be able to arrange refund guarantees,” in the words of Alex Sayegh of HFW, so the yards strong enough to provide one tend to be the ones least likely to get into financial difficulty. Where a guarantee exists, its expiry is commonly set against the contractual delivery date, so cover can lapse as a late build reaches its riskiest period, and a material variation agreed without the guarantor’s consent can void it (MacNally). The Florence order of 6 July showed that a restructuring court can freeze even an on-demand guarantee.

original_paragraph: Three workstreams the buyer’s team handles in advance. Yard financial due diligence at heads of terms: recent published accounts, parent structure, order-book composition, and litigation history form part of standard pre-contract assessment. Refund guarantee credit quality carries the same weight as any other contract term. And the buyer decides in advance, with counsel, what to do if mid-build distress produces an equity-injection or accelerated-payment proposal, so the decision is made before the pressure arrives. The contract can record that decision: a right to information on the yard’s financial condition at set intervals, a right to suspend payments on named warning signs (missed supplier payments, a rating downgrade, a covenant breach, a shareholder change), and step-in rights over the unfinished hull, materials, and design files so the vessel can be completed elsewhere (Maltby). The difficulty is timing. Termination clauses respond to formal events, the opening of proceedings or the appointment of an administrator, and yards file late. “Even where the owner can see that the yard is in trouble, it cannot take action under the contract,” Linda Roxburgh of Wikborg Rein wrote in 2024. The signs come earlier: prices cut to win deposits, senior technical staff leaving, suppliers asking whether the last instalment has been paid. TISG published its financial position monthly under a CONSOB order throughout its decline, and MacNally knows of no credit-monitoring service that reads such filings on a yacht buyer’s behalf.

original_paragraph: The third pattern is distinct from yard financial distress: a price below what the build can credibly be done for. Hein Velema, the first president of SYBAss, puts this test first when assessing a yard (see his interview in this chapter). In its members’ experience a major refit period within a five-year cycle can cost as much as a year’s operating budget. The guide keeps four budgets apart, annual maintenance, planned refit, regulatory works, and owner upgrades, so the owner can see whether the yacht is being looked after or simply spent on. Equipment fitted at the same time tends to fall due at the same time, and a ten-year cost profile drawn at purchase shows the clusters an annual average hides; giving every critical system a known end-of-support date turns obsolescence into a scheduled line item rather than a failure.
